\chapter{Weather}
\label{ch:la-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say it is raining, and name heat and sun in Latin, using its subjectless weather verbs.}

Say pluit with no subject at all, then name calor and sol, and check the pl- to ll- path into llueve.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tempestās]{tempestās — one Latin word widened, its own derivative narrowed}

\label{lesson:LA-C15-tempestas-pluit}



\begin{quote}
You've seen Spanish's \emph{tiempo} mean both \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} at once. Here's the honest history: Classical Latin actually kept these apart — but it wasn't Spanish that changed that. It happened inside Latin itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tempestās — a derivative of tempus, specialized for weather, then narrowed further}
\textbf{tempestās} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather, storm}\textquotedblright{} — grammatically a \textbf{derivative noun} built on \textbf{tempus} (\textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}), and by Classical Latin it had already \textbf{specialized}: \emph{tempus} stayed strictly \textquotedblleft{}time,\textquotedblright{} while \emph{tempestās} carried the weather/storm sense on its own. (English kept this split too: \emph{tempestās} gives \textbf{tempest}, \textquotedblleft{}a violent storm,\textquotedblright{} while \emph{tempus} gives \textbf{temporal, tempo}.)

Be careful with what happened next, though: Spanish's single \emph{tiempo} is \textbf{not} these two words merging back together. Later — still \textbf{within Latin's own history}, before Spanish, French, or Italian existed as separate languages — \textbf{tempus itself re-widened} to also cover \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} (that's why French \emph{temps} and Italian \emph{tempo} carry the exact same double sense; this happened at the shared Latin stage, not as a Spanish-only development). Meanwhile \emph{tempestās} kept going too, narrowing further to mean specifically \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{storm}\textquotedblright{} — and it's still alive in Spanish today as its own separate word, \textbf{tempestad} (\textquotedblleft{}storm, tempest\textquotedblright{}), sitting right alongside \emph{tiempo}. So it's one word (\emph{tempus}) widening back out, not two words fusing into one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tempestās\textquotedblright{} — weather/storm, a derivative of tempus, \textquotedblleft{}time,\textquotedblright{} narrowed today to Spanish's \textquotedblleft{}tempestad\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tempus\textquotedblright{} — time, later widened inside Latin to weather too
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Were \emph{tempus} and \emph{tempestās} the same word in Classical Latin? (\textbf{No} — \emph{tempestās} is a derivative that specialized for weather/storm, while \emph{tempus} stayed strictly \textquotedblleft{}time.\textquotedblright{}) Did Spanish merge these two words back together? (\textbf{No} — \emph{tempus} itself re-widened to cover \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} already within Latin's own history, shared by French/Italian too; \emph{tempestās} kept narrowing and survives separately as Spanish \emph{tempestad}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pluit, calor, sol]{pluit, calor, sol — three pieces of weather language}

\label{lesson:LA-C15-weather-verbs}



\begin{quote}
You know the history of \textbf{tempestās}. Now learn how Latin actually states rain, heat, and sun.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: pluit — a subjectless weather verb}]
Latin uses dedicated impersonal verbs with no subject at all:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pluit} — it rains
  \item \textbf{ningit} — it snows
  \item \textbf{tonat} — it thunders
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pluit} is the ancestor of Spanish \textbf{llueve}. Its opening follows the same \textbf{pl- $\to$ ll-} path as \emph{plovere $\to$ llover}, \emph{clāmāre $\to$ llamar}, and \emph{flamma $\to$ llama}.

This verb pattern resembles English \textquotedblleft{}it rains\textquotedblright{} more closely than Spanish \textbf{hace calor}. Spanish kept the dedicated verb for rain but built a new \textbf{hacer} expression for heat, cold, and sun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: calor and sol — carried straight through}
Latin \textbf{calor} (\textquotedblleft{}heat\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{sol} (\textquotedblleft{}sun\textquotedblright{}) are also Spanish \textbf{calor} and \textbf{sol}. These words needed no visible sound change at all.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pluit\textquotedblright{} — it rains; ancestor of Spanish llueve
  \item \textquotedblleft{}calor\textquotedblright{} — heat, unchanged in Spanish
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sol\textquotedblright{} — sun, unchanged in Spanish
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}it rains\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Pluit}, with no subject.) What sound path connects it to Spanish \textbf{llueve}? (\textbf{pl- $\to$ ll-}.) Which two weather nouns pass into Spanish unchanged? (\textbf{Calor} and \textbf{sol}.) Does Latin use a counterpart of Spanish \textbf{hacer} for all three ideas? (\textbf{No} — it uses dedicated impersonal weather verbs.)
\end{tcolorbox}
